content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Link the type of bonding to physical properties
Predict properties of substances from their bonding
Compare different types of structures and their properties
Explain properties using knowledge of structure and bonding
The properties of a substance depend directly on its structure and bonding. By understanding how atoms are bonded and arranged, we can predict and explain the properties of different materials.
Weak intermolecular forces easy to overcome
Many strong covalent bonds to break
*Graphite is an exception - it conducts due to delocalised electrons
No charged particles, molecules are neutral
Delocalised electrons always free to move
Substance X is a solid at room temperature, does not conduct electricity when solid, but does conduct when molten.
Does not conduct when solid → ions are fixed
Conducts when molten → ions can move
Substance Y has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity under any conditions.
Very high melting point → giant structure with strong bonds
Never conducts → no mobile electrons or ions
Giant covalent structure (like diamond or SiO₂)
Substance Z has a low melting point and does not conduct electricity.
Low melting point → weak forces between particles
Does not conduct → no charged particles

Is it a solid at room temperature with high melting point?
├── Yes → Does it conduct electricity when solid?
│   ├── Yes → METALLIC
│   └── No → Does it conduct when molten?
│       ├── Yes → IONIC
│       └── No → GIANT COVALENT
└── No (low melting point) → SIMPLE MOLECULAR
Predict and explain the properties of magnesium chloride (MgCl₂).
Therefore: Ionic bonding, giant ionic lattice
- strong electrostatic forces between Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
- rigid structure that shatters if layers shift
Saying covalent bonds break when a simple molecular substance melts
Only intermolecular forces are overcome; covalent bonds stay intact
Thinking high melting point always means ionic
Giant covalent and metallic structures also have high melting points
Forgetting that graphite is an exception
Graphite conducts electricity despite being giant covalent
A substance has a low melting point and does not conduct electricity. What type of structure does it have? Explain your answer. (3 marks)
Explain why magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride. (3 marks)
Graphite and diamond are both forms of carbon, but graphite conducts electricity while diamond does not. Explain why. (4 marks)
A substance conducts electricity when solid and can be bent into different shapes without breaking. What type of structure does it have? Explain your answer. (3 marks)
Small molecules with weak intermolecular forces
Many atoms bonded by strong covalent bonds
Many ions in a lattice with strong electrostatic forces
Positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons
Low mp/bp, no conduction, due to weak intermolecular forces
Very high mp/bp, no conduction (except graphite), very hard
High mp/bp, conducts when molten/dissolved, brittle
Usually high mp/bp, conducts solid and liquid, malleable/ductile
Properties can be predicted from structure, and structure can be deduced from properties
